papers_read.title_as_printed: Understanding the role of psychiatrists in the diagnosis and management of mild cognitive impairment and mild Alzheimer’s disease dementia: a cross‑sectional survey
papers_read.note: Gopalakrishna G, Brunton S, Pruzin J, Alford S, Hamersky C, Sabharwal A. BMC Psychiatry (2023) 23:716, doi 10.1186/s12888-023-05129-5; pages 1-8 of the regenerated ROOT/pdf/P-1017.txt. The first pack file for P-1017 was a different paper (Woodward et al., J Alzheimers Dis 89 (2022) 803-809, corpus P-979), from a PDF-map error the coordinator reports repaired; no verdict was formed on that text, and this adjudication rests only on the regenerated file.

papers_read.title_as_printed: Real‑life management of patients with mild cognitive impairment: an Italian survey
papers_read.note: Bonanni L, Cagnin A, Carrarini C, Logroscino G, Marra C, Rainero I. Neurol Sci (2024) 45:4279-4289, doi 10.1007/s10072-024-07478-9; pages 1-11. Supplementary materials 1-3 (centre list and survey items) are online only.

what_each_reports.P-1017: Anonymous online survey (4 February to 1 March 2021) of US physicians recruited from an opt-in research panel: 301 qualified, 50 of them psychiatrists (70% geriatric psychiatry, 56% neuropsychiatry interest), each required to have seen at least 25 MCI/mild AD patients in the past month. Psychiatrists report personally diagnosing 67% of their MCI/mild AD patients (9% referred for diagnosis, 23% previously diagnosed), using mental status testing (94%), medical history (86%), neurological exam (61%), blood tests (59%) and imaging (55%); 69% follow APA guidelines, 82% report advanced training, 92% receive referrals and 46% see themselves as care coordinator. All figures are self-report, not audited; the statement that psychiatrists 'can provide timely and accurate diagnosis' is the authors' conclusion, not a measured accuracy. Funded by Novo Nordisk, three authors being employees.
what_each_reports.P-1080: Two-phase survey of 121 Italian neurologists at 17 centres chosen by the scientific board for their MCI activity. Phase 1 (self-reported usual practice): 83.1% use the MCI category, 40.2% also use alternative criteria, 40% do not diagnose prodromal AD/MCI due to AD; MMSE used for screening by 93.3%, MoCA 57.1%, second-level neuropsychology 70.4%; brain MRI 97.5%, CT 62.4%, FDG-PET 52.5%, amyloid PET 45.2%, EEG 50%; routine laboratory tests 78.8-100%. Phase 2 (decisions recorded for 203 patients over 3 months): MMSE in 95.1%, MoCA 38.4%, MRI 80%, FDG-PET 21.1%, amyloid PET 5.9%. No agreement statistic or between-centre test. The verdict 'suboptimal management of MCI patients in Italy' is inferred from the heterogeneity of criteria, tests and treatments.

quantity_a: Self-reported share of their own MCI/mild AD caseload that high-volume US psychiatrists (n = 50) personally diagnose, and the proportions of those psychiatrists reporting given diagnostic methods, guideline use, training and a care-coordinator role.
quantity_b: Proportions of Italian neurologists (121, self-report) and of their patients (203, recorded decisions) with given diagnostic criteria, tests, imaging and treatments, read as between-clinician heterogeneity, and the authors' normative verdict that management is suboptimal.
incompatible_if_same: No. A panel of US psychiatrists who diagnose two-thirds of their caseload and an Italian neurologist sample with heterogeneous criteria can both be as reported. On the one item both surveys ask, use of a brief mental-status screen, they agree (94% of psychiatrists; MMSE for screening by 93.3% of neurologists). Items that differ numerically (imaging 55% versus brain MRI 97.5%; blood testing 59% versus routine laboratory tests 78.8-100%) compare different specialties in different countries with different item wording, so they are not estimates of one quantity, and neither paper claims the other's figure is wrong.

gates.task: match: T6 (clinician practice surveys, no model) in both, per registry.
gates.dataset_family: mismatch: a US commercial opt-in physician panel versus an Italian network of board-selected memory centres; two distinct samples, no waiver on record.
gates.validation_tier: n/a: two descriptive surveys that validate no model (counted as matched).
gates.modality_family: match at family level (clinician questionnaire), with different instruments: P-1080 adds a patient-level record of actual decisions (phase 2); P-1017 is a single practice-and-attitude questionnaire.

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: both report proportions, but of different units and items (share of a psychiatrist's own caseload personally diagnosed and share of psychiatrists endorsing a method or role, versus share of neurologists or of patients with a given criterion, test or treatment); the one common item, a brief cognitive screen, gives concordant proportions.
independence: independent: different countries, specialties, samples and author teams; both industry-supported, by different sponsors (Novo Nordisk for P-1017; an unconditional PIAM grant for P-1080).
grounds: P-1017 measures who diagnoses and with which self-reported tools in a panel of 50 high-volume US psychiatrists [q1, q2, q3, q4].
P-1080 measures how uniform diagnostic and therapeutic practice is among Italian neurologists at board-selected centres and infers suboptimal management from that heterogeneity [q7, q8, q9, q10].

The favourable and unfavourable verdicts concern different clinician populations and different constructs, and P-1080 itself excluded psychiatrists, so a claim about one cannot contradict the claim about the other [q5, q12].
Where both surveys ask the same question, use of a brief mental-status screen, they agree (94% versus 93.3%) [q2, q11].

The record's statement that P-1080 reports no percentage is wrong, but the percentages it does report describe Italian neurologists or their patients, not US psychiatrists, so they form no incompatible pair [q10, q11].

evidence_quotes.quote: A total of 301 physicians participated in the survey, 50 of whom were psychiatrists.

Of their patients with all-cause MCI or mild AD dementia, psychiatrists reported personally diagnosing two-thirds (67%). Psychiatrists used various methods to diagnose MCI or mild AD dementia including mental status testing (94%)
HCPs who had previously opted in to participate in online research surveys were recruited via email.
Most respondents reported subspecializing in geriatric psychiatry (70%) or neuropsychiatry (56%).
They can provide timely and accurate diagnosis of clinical MCI and mild AD dementia and develop optimal treatment plans for patients.
Self-reporting is a limitation inherent to survey-based research.

Information gathered in the first phase of the survey highlighted a non-uniform use of diagnostic criteria and procedures for MCI, as well as a very heterogeneous therapeutic strategy among Italian neurologists.
The results of our study reflect a suboptimal management of MCI patients in Italy and highlight the need of standardized diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for this condition.
Selected clinicians were deliberately chosen based on their experience in the management of patients with MCI.
Most neurologists (88.6%) reported to visit often (several times per month) patients with MCI, and 83.1% reported to use the diagnostic category of MCI.
the neuropsychological test most frequently used for screening (93.3%), followed by Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) (57.1%).
the survey to neurologists alone, thereby excluding geriatricians and psychiatrists who are also involved in the identification and care of MCI patients
were deliberately chosen based on their involvement in the management of patients with MCI
the proposed Italian guidelines for a biological diagnosis of MCI [13]
Almost one-third of patients suspected of having MCI or mild AD dementia are referred to specialists including psychiatrists.
Psychiatrists reported most commonly following the American Psychiatric Association guidelines (69%) for treatment of MCI and mild AD dementia.

record_defects: conflict_statement: 'P-1080 reports no percentage, agreement statistic or between-centre test for any of its claims, so no gap magnitude exists': P-1080 prints many percentages (Table 1: MMSE 93.3%, MoCA 57.1%, second-level neuropsychology 70.4%, brain MRI 97.5%; Table 2: MMSE in 95.1% of patients; 83.1% use the MCI category). It reports no agreement statistic or between-centre test, which is right [q10, q11].

claim_b: '17 self-selected Italian memory/neurology centres': the board invited 17 centres 'deliberately chosen' for their MCI activity and all accepted; clinicians were also chosen for experience. The sample is selected, not self-selected (still non-random) [q9, q13].

The P-1017 evidence quote 'Psychiatrists already diagnose and manage most MCI/mild AD patients they see but do not perceive themselves as care coordinators, exposing a coordination gap in the care pathway.' and the inference that P-1017's 'own conclusion is itself a gap finding' are summary-block wording; the paper's conclusion is favourable ('They can provide timely and accurate diagnosis ...') and mentions the coordinator point as a qualification. The incommensurability does not rest on that reading [q5].

Other quotes attributed to the papers ('Opt-in online survey panel; modest psychiatrist cell (n=50); ...'; 'Descriptive: 121 neurologists, 203 patients; ...'; 'Survey-based, descriptive design; self-selected participating centres/neurologists; ...'; 'MCI is clinically heterogeneous ... non-uniform or absent') are summary-block or registry wording, not PDF text; 'About one-third of patients ...' paraphrases the paper's 'Almost one-third of patients suspected of having MCI or mild AD dementia are referred to specialists including psychiatrists.' [q15].
'a US specialty in which 82% of respondents report advanced formal MCI/AD training': the 82% is of the 50 psychiatrists, not of all 301 respondents.

'The Italian setting is a stated guideline-absent regime': P-1080 says there is no unanimously accepted practical guidance, but also refers to 'the proposed Italian guidelines for a biological diagnosis of MCI'; 'guideline-absent' overstates [q14].

'pass all four deterministic comparability gates': those are the gatecheck columns; under the review's four gates the dataset-family gate fails (a US panel versus an Italian centre network), with no waiver on record.
what_would_change_the_verdict: Two surveys estimating the same proportion in the same class of clinicians (for example, the share of neurologists who personally make the MCI diagnosis, or who use a named test or criterion), with estimates whose uncertainty excludes each other and a claim in one paper that the other contradicts; nothing in these two papers does that.
